clue.text: First to span river in Dodge

indicators.note: 'first to' points at only the opening letter of the following word

blocks.note: opening letter of span
the Cam is the river through Cambridge

explanation.surface: Someone is told to bridge a river in Dodge City first.
explanation.walkthrough: Dodge reads like the American town but is the definition, a noun for a con.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodge is a crafty trick or swindle, which is what a scam is.

clue.text: Sea Denizen can perform on track

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece placed on another sits above it, so the next word follows

blocks.note: can and john are both slang for a toilet
to do is to perform
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A sea creature turns out able to perform on a racetrack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb, but it is the slang noun for a lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: The John Dory is an edible marine fish, so it is literally an inhabitant of the sea.

clue.text: They say your writer will land in water

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than read, so the sound matters

blocks.note: your writer is the setter, I, and 'I will' contracts to I'll

explanation.surface: People predict that the author is going to come down in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your writer' is the crossword setter speaking of themself as I.
explanation.definitionFit: An isle is an island, a piece of land surrounded by water.

clue.text: Branch Indy news supremo protected

blocks.note: a branch of a service or organisation is an arm
the Independent (Indy) is the setter's paper, so its editor is OUR ED

explanation.surface: A regional office's head of news at the Independent was shielded.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter writes for the Independent, nicknamed the Indy, so its editor is 'our ed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Armoured means covered with protective plating, so something armoured is protected.

clue.text: Two females in AA with Irish pigeon

indicators.note: one thing in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female, twice
taken as written, split around the females
IR is the abbreviation for Irish

explanation.surface: Two women at Alcoholics Anonymous accompanied by an Irish pigeon.
explanation.walkthrough: AA here is just two letters, not Alcoholics Anonymous. 'Not my pigeon' is a British idiom meaning not my business.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom 'that's your pigeon', a pigeon is one's concern or business, as is one's affair.

clue.text: Short fat kid visits relations

indicators.note: something short is cut off before its end, so the final letter goes
a visitor goes inside someone's home, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: grease is fat, docked of its last letter
to kid someone is to tease or taunt them

explanation.surface: A small, plump child calls on family members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short fat kid' reads as one chubby child, but short trims the fat and kid is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-aunt is a parent's aunt, so great-aunts are kinsfolk.

clue.text: Mystery mage swimming round North Island

indicators.note: something swimming moves about freely, so the letters are rearranged
going round something means surrounding it

blocks.note: the four letters of mage rearranged
N is the abbreviation for north
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A puzzling wizard is seen bathing around an island to the north.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is a puzzle or something baffling, the same as a mystery.

clue.text: Bank simply ignoring me

indicators.note: ignoring something leaves it out of account, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: simply and merely both mean only
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A bank that simply pays no attention to the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Bank is a verb here, as in 'bank on'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to depend on them, so bank and rely share that verb sense.

clue.text: See 12

blocks.note: the answer at 12 means mad, and so does cross
'see' in a book directs to a reference

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is itself a pointer to another entry, while 12's answer means cross and 'see' is a reference; 12 comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-reference is an instruction such as 'see 12' directing the reader to another place.

clue.text: See 9
State brief time at sea not bad

indicators.note: something gone bad is spoiled and out of order, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: MIN is the short form of minute
both words taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor declares that a short spell at sea wasn't too awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' looks like the anagram signal, but sea is fodder and 'bad' does the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnesota is one of the United States, a state in the Upper Midwest.

clue.text: Mad King George some must admit

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: some and any are both indefinite quantity words
GR, Georgius Rex, is King George's royal cipher

explanation.surface: Some people have to concede that King George III was insane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad King George' suggests George III, but Mad is the definition. GR is the cipher on British post boxes for George Rex.
explanation.definitionFit: Mad in its informal sense of furious is a synonym of angry.

clue.text: Kangaroo eating large crusty loaf

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater

blocks.note: a boomer is a large male kangaroo in Australia
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A kangaroo tucks into a big crusty loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Boomer is Australian slang for a big male kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a British bread loaf with a thick crust and slashed top.

clue.text: Listening device left in: note something sticking out

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a bug is a hidden microphone
L is the abbreviation for left
E is a note of the musical scale

explanation.surface: A microphone was planted inside; note something protruding.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulge is a swelling or protrusion that sticks out from a surface.

clue.text: Sausage roll made at Barking

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go crazy

blocks.note: the three words taken as written

explanation.surface: A sausage roll was produced in Barking, a district of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is an east London district, and also British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortadella is a large Italian pork sausage from Bologna, served sliced.

clue.text: Something genuine in the round?

blocks.note: surface: something authentic, perhaps a sculpture or play staged in the round
setter's reading: an authentic beer ordered as part of a round of drinks at the pub

explanation.walkthrough: A round is the set of drinks one person buys for a group in a British pub; the genuine thing is cask-conditioned beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Real ale is traditional cask beer, championed as the authentic article and bought by the pint in rounds.

clue.text: Sheep must guard river vessels

indicators.note: guarding something means surrounding and enclosing it

blocks.note: ewes are female sheep
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Sheep have to keep watch over boats on the river.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug, a container, so ewers are vessels in that sense.

clue.text: Productive hen always held in both hands

indicators.note: what is held in something sits within it

blocks.note: L and R, left and right
aye is an old and Scottish word for always

explanation.surface: A hen that lays well is forever cradled in two hands.
explanation.walkthrough: Aye meaning ever, as in 'for aye', is a poetic word.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer is a hen kept for producing eggs, so a productive one.

clue.text: Fish turned around

indicators.note: going around means turning to face the other way

blocks.note: milk that has turned has gone off

explanation.surface: A fish swung round in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned around' reads as one phrase, but turned means went off, as milk does.
explanation.definitionFit: The dab is a small flatfish found in European coastal waters.

clue.text: Money from toads curse protects

indicators.note: protecting something means wrapping around it

blocks.note: a bane is a curse or affliction
a knot is the collective noun for a group of toads

explanation.surface: Cash obtained from toads is guarded by a curse, like a fairy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Knot is the collective noun for toads, as flock is for sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: A banknote is a piece of paper currency, so it is money.

clue.text: Med resort accommodates hotel in suitable place

indicators.note: a place that accommodates a guest holds them inside

blocks.note: Nice is a resort on the French Mediterranean coast
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Riviera resort puts up a hotel in a well-chosen spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a position or role that suits someone well, a fitting spot.

clue.text: Mexican politician once cooked with lard

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former Mexican leader used to fry with lard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' looks like it means former, attached to the politician, but its letters are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Felipe Calderón was President of Mexico from 2006 to 2012.

clue.text: Aged men supply drama with bins

indicators.note: supply here is the adverb of supple, so the letters bend into a new order

blocks.note: both words taken as written

explanation.surface: Old men provide a theatre piece featuring dustbins.
explanation.walkthrough: Supply looks like the verb to provide, but it is pronounced supp-lee, meaning in a supple way.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's play Endgame famously keeps two elderly characters in dustbins on stage.

clue.text: Test for one newly off the drink?

definitions.text: for one newly off the drink?

blocks.note: first meaning: a rehearsal or trial

blocks.clueFragment: for one newly off the drink?
blocks.note: second meaning, whimsically: a stretch without alcohol for a person who has just stopped

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second sense: someone who has gone dry is on a run of sobriety.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry run is a practice trial before the real thing, so it is a test.

clue.text: Fish gobbling fellow up in coat

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom
what is gobbled ends up inside the gobbler

blocks.note: an eel is a fish
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A fish wolfing down a man who is wearing a coat.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is a glossy paint or glaze applied as a coat on a surface.

clue.text: Swiss food company's lies close up

blocks.note: first meaning: belonging to Nestlé, the Swiss food giant
second meaning: snuggles in

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a corporate deception; lies is the verb to recline.
explanation.definitionFit: Nestlé's is the possessive of the Swiss multinational, and to nestle is to settle snugly against someone.

clue.text: Writer in rapture brought to church ...

indicators.note: bringing one thing to another sets them side by side

blocks.note: rapture is intense joy
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: An author in ecstasy is taken to church.
explanation.definitionFit: James Joyce was the Irish novelist who wrote Ulysses, so a writer.

clue.text: Comedian losing stone makes gibe

indicators.note: losing something means it is no longer there, so letters drop out

blocks.note: a jester is a comic entertainer
ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight

explanation.surface: A comic who slims down makes a sneering remark.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of body weight, fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeer is a mocking taunt, the same as a gibe.

clue.text: ... and back, into a Mitford-approved vein to the point of producing disgust?

definitions.text: to the point of producing disgust?

indicators.note: going back means running the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
Nancy Mitford popularised U for upper-class usage
a seam is a vein of ore or coal

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a writer goes back into an upper-class mood until it sickens.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to 26, but this clue stands alone. Nancy Mitford's essay labelled genteel speech U and its opposite non-U.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad nauseam means continuing to a sickening, tedious degree, the extent that causes disgust.

clue.text: Take lead from unusually large boss

indicators.note: the lead is the front, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: jumbo means extra large

explanation.surface: An oversized employer gets told to set an example.
explanation.walkthrough: Boss looks like an employer, but it is the raised stud at the centre of a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbo is the round projecting knob in the middle of a shield, also called its boss.

clue.text: It was appropriate to get together

definitions.note: the clue gives the archaic sense, 'it was' flagging an old usage

blocks.note: first meaning: an old adjective for fitting
second meaning: to assemble or encounter

explanation.walkthrough: 'It was' warns that the first sense is old-fashioned, surviving in the prayer-book phrase 'meet and right'.
explanation.definitionFit: In older English the adjective meant suitable or proper; as a verb it means assemble.

clue.text: Net at sea to keep cows mostly buoyant

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and lost, so the letters are muddled
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter goes
keeping something means holding it within

blocks.note: the three letters rearranged
to cow someone is to bully them

explanation.surface: A fishing net on the ocean holding cattle mostly stays afloat.
explanation.walkthrough: Cows looks like cattle, but it is the verb meaning intimidates.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyant in its figurative sense means cheerful and lively, as does ebullient.

clue.text: Hard stuff in black and slimy mud?

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
ooze is soft wet mud, as on a seabed

explanation.surface: Something solid lies in dark, slippery mud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard stuff' suggests something solid; it is the slang for strong spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard stuff is slang for strong liquor, and booze is a casual word for alcohol.
